title: Security Models
objective: Study-guide review — CISSP — Domain 3: Security Architecture and Engineering: Security Models.

items: Foundation for many formal security models
System is always in a defined state (set of permissions and access)
Secure state — all access permissions are controlled and enforced
State transitions must maintain security invariants
Bell-LaPadula and Biba are built on the state machine model

blocks.text: From Shon Harris: "The developer must define a secure state for each state variable. The next step is to define and identify the allowable state transition functions. These functions will describe how the system transitions between states while maintaining security." A system is in a secure state when:

items: All subjects can only access objects they are authorized to access
All state transitions maintain the security properties
No unauthorized information flow can occur
Focuses on CONFIDENTIALITY (protects against unauthorized disclosure)
Simple Security Property ("No Read Up") — Subject cannot read above their clearance
Star (*) Property ("No Write Down") — Subject cannot write to a lower classification
Strong Star Property — Subject can only read/write at their own level
Does NOT address integrity

blocks.text: From Chapple: "The Bell-LaPadula properties are in place to protect data confidentiality. A subject cannot read an object that is classified at a higher level than the subject is cleared for."

From Shon Harris: "The Bell-LaPadula model deals only with confidentiality, while the Biba and Clark-Wilson models deal only with integrity." Mnemonic: Bell-LaPadula = "BLP = Be Low for Peace" (you can't read up, can't write down — keeps secrets UP) ⚠️ Exam Trap: Bell-LaPadula is CONFIDENTIALITY only. It says nothing about integrity. A user can write to a higher level (star property allows write up), which could corrupt data at higher levels. This is why Biba exists.

items: Focuses on INTEGRITY (protects against unauthorized modification)
Simple Integrity Property ("No Read Down") — Subject cannot read from lower integrity
Star (*) Integrity Property ("No Write Up") — Subject cannot write to higher integrity
Inverse of Bell-LaPadula
Does NOT address confidentiality

blocks.text: Mnemonic: Biba = "Biba = Basically Integrity" — No Read Down, No Write Up (protects integrity by keeping lower-quality data from contaminating higher levels) Comparison:

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.text: ⚠️ Exam Trap: Bell-LaPadula and Biba are INVERSES of each other. Bell-LaPadula: No Read Up, No Write Down. Biba: No Read Down, No Write Up. The exam frequently tests this distinction.

items: Focuses on INTEGRITY through well-formed transactions
Uses Constrained Data Items (CDIs) — data protected by the model
Unconstrained Data Items (UDIs) — data not yet validated
Transformation Procedures (TPs) — only authorized operations that can modify CDIs
Integrity Verification Procedures (IVPs) — verify CDI integrity

blocks.text: From Stewart: "An integrity verification procedure (IVP) is a procedure that scans data items and confirms their integrity. Transformation procedures (TPs) are the only procedures that are allowed to modify a CDI." Clark-Wilson is more practical than Biba for commercial environments because:

items: It enforces well-formed transactions (like accounting double-entry bookkeeping)
Users access data only through authorized programs (TPs)
Separation of duties is built into the model
It's the closest model to how real commercial systems work

blocks.text: Key Concept: Users never access CDIs directly — they must go through TPs. This is similar to how database applications work: users interact with the application (TP), not the database directly.

items: Also called the Chinese Wall model
Prevents conflicts of interest by dynamically controlling access
Once a user accesses data from one competitor, they're blocked from accessing data from rival competitors
Used in financial, legal, and consulting environments
Access restrictions are dynamic — they change based on prior access history

blocks.text: Example: A consulting firm advises both Coca-Cola and Pepsi. Once a consultant accesses Coca-Cola's data, they are automatically prevented from accessing Pepsi's data (and vice versa). This prevents conflict of interest and information leakage between competitors. The model addresses both confidentiality and integrity through conflict-of-interest classes.

items: Graham-Denning — Defines 8 primitive protection rights for subjects and objects
Addresses how to create, delete, and transfer access rights securely
Harrison-Ruzzo-Ullman (HRU) — Extension of Graham-Denning with formal access matrix
Both address the access control matrix concept
Focus on the secure management of access rights
Create object
Create subject
Delete object
Delete subject
Read access rights
Grant access rights
Delete access rights
Transfer access rights

blocks.text: These models formalize how access control decisions are made and managed, forming the theoretical foundation for modern access control systems.

Simple Security Property ("No Read Up"): Subject cannot read above their clearance
Star (*) Property ("No Write Down"): Subject cannot write to a lower classification
Strong Star Property: Subject can only read/write at their own level
Strong Star: Read/Write only at own level
Simple Integrity Property ("No Read Down"): Subject cannot read from lower integrity
Star (*) Integrity Property ("No Write Up"): Subject cannot write to higher integrity
